modern_osis:
Jonah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Jonah came from Galilee (2 Kings 14:25).

His miraculous rescue from the fish made him a type of our blessed Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus himself referred to the event, thereby affirming that the narrative is true.

For the almighty Creator and Sustainer of life, everything described in the book was possible.

The example of the people of Nineveh shows the abundance of God's patience and forbearance toward sinners.

The book also presents a sharp contrast between God's mercy and goodness and his servant's disobedience, impatience and irritability.

Those who know their own hearts best will understand its lessons most deeply.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJonah, sent to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish.1–3He is stayed by a tempest.4–7His discourse with the mariners.8–12He is cast into the sea, and miraculously preserved.13–17
Jonah flees from his calling (verses 1–3)

How sad it is to think of the great amount of sin committed in the world's large cities!

The wickedness of Nineveh was an open and defiant insult to God.

Jonah was commanded to go there immediately and warn the people publicly.

But he refused.

Few of us can honestly claim we would have eagerly accepted such a dangerous mission without hesitation.

Jonah found what looked like a providential opportunity to escape.

But a person can be outside the path of duty and still receive a favorable wind.

The easiest route is not always the right one.

See how even the best human beings can act when God leaves them to themselves.

When we hear God's commands, we also need the Holy Spirit to bring our thoughts into submission to his will.

The storm awakens the sailors (verses 4–7)

God sent a terrible storm in pursuit of Jonah.

Sin brings storms into souls, households, churches and whole nations.

It disturbs and destroys peace.

The sailors cried out to their gods and also did everything they could to save the ship.

If only people showed as much wisdom about their souls!

They would gladly part with the wealth, pleasure and honor they cannot keep without destroying faith, conscience and ultimately salvation.

Meanwhile, Jonah slept deeply.

Sin makes people numb and careless.

We must beware of hearts hardened by its deceitfulness.

What are sinners thinking when they sleep on despite the warnings of Scripture and conscience?

We should awaken one another and encourage everyone to call on God for deliverance.

The sailors concluded that the disaster had some moral cause.

Whatever affliction we experience, we should ask the Lord what we need to learn from it.

The lot fell upon Jonah.

God has many ways of uncovering sins and sinners that everyone imagined were safely hidden.

Jonah confesses before the sailors (verses 8–12)

Jonah explained his faith.

Henry hopes he did so with sorrow and shame, confessing his guilt and honoring God's justice.

He taught the sailors about Jehovah, the Maker of sea and land.

They challenged him:

If he feared the Creator of land and sea, why had he imagined he could flee from God's presence?

When people who profess religion act wrongly, even those who do not profess it may justly rebuke them.

When sin has stirred a storm, we must address the sin that caused it.

Jonah spoke like a truly repentant person who does not want other people to suffer because of personal folly.

He accepted the sentence and acknowledged God's justice.

A guilty conscience will find no genuine peace until it abandons the sin that has troubled it.

Simply surrendering money or possessions cannot cleanse the conscience.

In the image of this account, Jonah himself must be thrown overboard.

Jonah is thrown into the sea and preserved (verses 13–17)

The sailors tried rowing against the wind of God's displeasure and the current of his purpose.

But it was useless to seek safety without dealing with the cause of the judgment.

Even an ordinary human conscience naturally fears becoming guilty of another person's death.

When God leads us through his Providence, we ought to be satisfied with his wise purposes, even when they are difficult for us to accept.

The storm stopped when Jonah was cast into the sea.

God does not discipline forever.

His correction lasts until his purpose is fulfilled and his people submit to him.

The pagan sailors may rise in judgment against many people called Christians who offer neither prayer in distress nor thanksgiving after deliverance.

The Lord commands every creature.

He can make any of them an instrument of mercy toward his people.

How wonderful his power in preserving a drowning man, and how great his pity in preserving one who had fled from and offended him!

It was because of the Lord's mercy that Jonah was not destroyed.

He remained alive in the fish for three days and three nights.

This was impossible by ordinary natural means, but everything is possible for the God who rules nature.

Jonah's preservation made him a type of Christ, as Jesus expressly taught in Matthew 12:40.
classic_reading:
[Jonah.1.1-Jonah.1.3]
Jonah
Jonah was a native of Galilee, [2Kgs.14.25] 2Ki 14:25. His miraculous deliverance from out of the fish, rendered him a type of our blessed Lord, who mentions it, so as to show the certain truth of the narrative. All that was done was easy to the almighty power of the Author and Sustainer of life. This book shows us, by the example of the Ninevites, how great are the Divine forbearance and long-suffering towards sinners. It shows a most striking contrast between the goodness and mercy of God, and the rebellion, impatience, and peevishness of his servant; and it will be best understood by those who are most acquainted with their own hearts.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Jonah, sent to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish. | (1-3) |
He is stayed by a tempest. | (4-7) |
His discourse with the mariners. | (8-12) |
He is cast into the sea, and miraculously preserved. | (13-17) |
Verses 1-3
It is sad to think how much sin is committed in great cities. Their wickedness, as that of Nineveh, is a bold and open affront to God. Jonah must go at once to Nineveh, and there, on the spot, cry against the wickedness of it. Jonah would not go. Probably there are few among us who would not have tried to decline such a mission. Providence seemed to give him an opportunity to escape; we may be out of the way of duty, and yet may meet with a favourable gale. The ready way is not always the right way. See what the best of men are, when God leaves them to themselves; and what need we have, when the word of the Lord comes to us, to have the Spirit of the Lord to bring every thought within us into obedience.
[Jonah.1.4-Jonah.1.7]
Verses 4-7
God sent a pursuer after Jonah, even a mighty tempest. Sin brings storms and tempests into the soul, into the family, into churches and nations; it is a disquieting, disturbing thing. Having called upon their gods for help, the sailors did what they could to help themselves. Oh that men would be thus wise for their souls, and would be willing to part with that wealth, pleasure, and honour, which they cannot keep without making shipwreck of faith and a good conscience, and ruining their souls for ever! Jonah was fast asleep. Sin is stupifying, and we are to take heed lest at any time our hearts are hardened by the deceitfulness of it. What do men mean by sleeping on in sin, when the word of God and the convictions of their own consciences, warn them to arise and call on the Lord, if they would escape everlasting misery? Should not we warn each other to awake, to arise, to call upon our God, if so be he will deliver us? The sailors concluded the storm was a messenger of Divine justice sent to some one in that ship. Whatever evil is upon us at any time, there is a cause for it; and each must pray, Lord, show me wherefore thou contendest with me. The lot fell upon Jonah. God has many ways of bringing to light hidden sins and sinners, and making manifest that folly which was thought to be hid from the eyes of all living.
[Jonah.1.8-Jonah.1.12]
Verses 8-12
Jonah gave an account of his religion, for that was his business. We may hope that he told with sorrow and shame, justifying God, condemning himself, and explaining to the mariners what a great God Jehovah is. They said to him, Why hast thou done this? If thou fearest the God that made the sea and the dry land, why wast thou such a fool as to think thou couldst flee from his presence? If the professors of religion do wrong, they will hear it from those who make no such profession. When sin has raised a storm, and laid us under the tokens of God's displeasure, we must consider what is to be done to the sin that raised the storm. Jonah uses the language of true penitents, who desire that none but themselves may fare the worse for their sins and follies. Jonah sees this to be the punishment of his iniquity, he accepts it, and justifies God in it. When conscience is awakened, and a storm raised, nothing will turn it into a calm but parting with the sin that caused the disturbance. Parting with our money will not pacify the conscience, the Jonah must be thrown overboard.
[Jonah.1.13-Jonah.1.17]
Verses 13-17
The mariners rowed against wind and tide, the wind of God's displeasure, the tide of his counsel; but it is in vain to think of saving ourselves any other way than by destroying our sins. Even natural conscience cannot but dread blood-guiltiness. And when we are led by Providence God does what he pleases, and we ought to be satisfied, though it may not please us. Throwing Jonah into the sea put an end to the storm. God will not afflict for ever, He will only contend till we submit and turn from our sins. Surely these heathen mariners will rise up in judgment against many called Christians, who neither offer prayers when in distress, nor thanksgiving for signal deliverances. The Lord commands all creatures, and can make any of them serve his designs of mercy to his people. Let us see this salvation of the Lord, and admire his power, that he could thus save a drowning man, and his pity, that he would thus save one who was running from him, and had offended him. It was of the Lord's mercies that Jonah was not consumed. Jonah was alive in the fish three days and nights: to nature this was impossible, but to the God of nature all things are possible. Jonah, by this miraculous preservation, was made a type of Christ; as our blessed Lord himself declared, [Matt.12.40] Mt 12:40.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe prayer of Jonah.1–9He is delivered from the fish.10
Jonah prays in the fish (verses 1–9)

Consider when Jonah prayed.

He was in distress, experiencing God's displeasure because of his disobedience.

We should pray whenever we suffer.

He had been preserved alive by a miracle and now turned to God.

Knowing that God still regards us with kindness, despite our wrongdoing, gives us courage to pray when fear of judgment has kept us silent.

Consider where he prayed: inside the great fish.

No place is unsuitable for prayer.

People may separate us from one another, but they cannot separate us from fellowship with God.

Consider whom he addressed: the Lord his God.

That encourages even people who have wandered away from their faith to return.

Consider the nature of his prayer.

The words recorded here seem to recount Jonah's experience and later reflections, rather than reproduce the exact words he said at every moment inside the fish.

He remembered how earnestly he had cried out, and how readily God had heard and answered him.

If we are to benefit from suffering, we must recognize God's hand in it.

Jonah had fled wickedly from the Lord's presence.

God could justly have withdrawn his Holy Spirit from him and never returned to him.

Only those from whom God withdraws his favor completely are truly miserable.

Jonah was perplexed but not without hope.

When he sought and trusted God in trouble, he experienced mercy.

He urged others to remain close to the Lord.

People who abandon their duty also abandon the comforts associated with fulfilling it.

As far as believers copy people who worship false things, they turn away from their own mercy and live beneath the privileges God has given them.

But Jonah's experience encourages believers in every age to trust the Lord as the God of salvation.

Jonah is released (verse 10)

Jonah's deliverance demonstrates God's power over every created thing.

It also displays his mercy toward a repentant sinner who prayed in trouble.

And it serves as a type of Christ's resurrection.

Through every change in circumstances, let us fix our faith upon our Redeemer who suffered and died, but has now risen and ascended.

Confess our sins.

Regard Christ's resurrection as a pledge of our own.

Receive every earthly and spiritual deliverance with thanks as a foretaste of eternal redemption.
classic_reading:
[Jonah.2.1-Jonah.2.9]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The prayer of Jonah. | (1-9) |
He is delivered from the fish. | (10) |
Verses 1-9
Observe when Jonah prayed. When he was in trouble, under the tokens of God's displeasure against him for sin: when we are in affliction we must pray. Being kept alive by miracle, he prayed. A sense of God's good-will to us, notwithstanding our offences, opens the lips in prayer, which were closed with the dread of wrath. Also, where he prayed; in the belly of the fish. No place is amiss for prayer. Men may shut us from communion with one another, but not from communion with God. To whom he prayed; to the Lord his God. This encourages even backsliders to return. What his prayer was. This seems to relate his experience and reflections, then and afterwards, rather than to be the form or substance of his prayer. Jonah reflects on the earnestness of his prayer, and God's readiness to hear and answer. If we would get good by our troubles, we must notice the hand of God in them. He had wickedly fled from the presence of the Lord, who might justly take his Holy Spirit from him, never to visit him more. Those only are miserable, whom God will no longer own and favour. But though he was perplexed, yet not in despair. Jonah reflects on the favour of God to him, when he sought to God, and trusted in him in his distress. He warns others, and tells them to keep close to God. Those who forsake their own duty, forsake their own mercy; those who run away from the work of their place and day, run away from the comfort of it. As far as a believer copies those who observe lying vanities, he forsakes his own mercy, and lives below his privileges. But Jonah's experience encourages others, in all ages, to trust in God, as the God of salvation.
[Jonah.2.10]
Verse 10
Jonah's deliverance may be considered as an instance of God's power over all the creatures. As an instance of God's mercy to a poor penitent, who in distress prays to him: and as a type and figure of Christ's resurrection. Amidst all our varying experiences, and the changing scenes of life; we should look by faith, fixedly, upon our once suffering and dying, but now risen and ascended Redeemer. Let us confess our sins, consider Christ's resurrection as an earnest of our own, and thankfully receive every temporal and spiritual deliverance, as the pledge of our eternal redemption.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJonah sent again to Nineveh, preaches there.1–4Nineveh is spared upon the repentance of the inhabitants.5–10
Jonah returns to his calling (verses 1–4)

God employed Jonah again.

The Lord's willingness to use us in his work is evidence of peace restored between us and him.

Jonah was no longer rebellious.

He did not avoid hearing the command or refuse to carry it out.

This is what genuine repentance looks like: a changed mind and conduct, a return to assigned work and duty.

Suffering can benefit us by bringing us back to the service we abandoned.

But that change displays divine grace, because suffering by itself is more likely to drive sinners away from God than to draw them to him.

The Lord's servants must go where he sends them, come when he calls, and do what he commands.

Jonah faithfully and boldly delivered his message.

Henry says it is uncertain whether Jonah added more explanation about God's anger or simply repeated the announcement.

Its central meaning is clear.

Forty days is a long delay for a righteous God to allow before judgment, but it is little time for sinful people to repent and reform.

The announcement should make us think seriously about preparation for death.

We cannot be as confident that we will live forty days as Nineveh was that it would endure for forty days.

We would be frightened if told with certainty we had less than a month to live, yet often remain indifferent though we cannot guarantee another day.

The Ninevites repent and are spared (verses 5–10)

The repentance and reform of Nineveh were a marvel of God's grace.

The people condemned later generations that heard the gospel and did not repent (Matthew 12:41).

Even limited knowledge about God can convince people that humility, confession, prayer and turning from sin are necessary in seeking mercy.

The people followed their king's example.

The repentance became national, as was necessary when the announced judgment concerned the whole nation.

Even the cries of animals deprived of food should remind their owners to cry to God.

When praying, we must cry earnestly, with fixed attention, strong faith and sincere affection.

Every part of the heart should be involved.

It is not enough to fast because of sin.

We must fast from sin.

If we cherish evil inwardly, our prayers cannot be sincere (Psalm 66:18).

A day's appointed fast does not complete the work of repentance when the day is over.

The Ninevites hoped that God would turn from his anger.

They had less certainty of finding mercy than Christians now possess through the death and merits of Jesus Christ, the foundation of pardon for those who repent.

They dared not presume upon grace, but they did not despair.

The hope of mercy is a powerful encouragement to sincere reform.

Let us humbly cast ourselves upon God's free grace.

He sees who actually turn from evil and who continue in it.

That is why he spared Nineveh.

The account records no sacrifices offered to provide atonement.

But God did not despise broken and contrite hearts.
classic_reading:
[Jonah.3.1-Jonah.3.4]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
Jonah sent again to Nineveh, preaches there. | (1-4) |
Nineveh is spared upon the repentance of the inhabitants. | (5-10) |
Verses 1-4
God employs Jonah again in his service. His making use of us is an evidence of his being at peace with us. Jonah was not disobedient, as he had been. He neither endeavoured to avoid hearing the command, nor declined to obey it. See here the nature of repentance; it is the change of our mind and way, and a return to our work and duty. Also, the benefit of affliction; it brings those back to their place who had deserted it. See the power of Divine grace, for affliction of itself would rather drive men from God, than draw them to him. God's servants must go where he sends them, come when he calls them, and do what he bids them; we must do whatever the word of the Lord commands. Jonah faithfully and boldly delivered his errand. Whether Jonah said more, to show the anger of God against them, or whether he only repeated these words again and again, is not certain, but this was the purport of his message. Forty days is a long time for a righteous God to delay judgments, yet it is but a little time for an unrighteous people to repent and reform in. And should it not awaken us to get ready for death, to consider that we cannot be so sure that we shall live forty days, as Nineveh then was that it should stand forty days? We should be alarmed if we were sure not to live a month, yet we are careless though we are not sure to live a day.
[Jonah.3.5-Jonah.3.10]
Verses 5-10
There was a wonder of Divine grace in the repentance and reformation of Nineveh. It condemns the men of the gospel generation, [Matt.12.41] Mt 12:41. A very small degree of light may convince men that humbling themselves before God, confessing their sins with prayer, and turning from sin, are means of escaping wrath and obtaining mercy. The people followed the example of the king. It became a national act, and it was necessary it should be so, when it was to prevent a national ruin. Let even the brute creatures' cries and moans for want of food remind their owners to cry to God. In prayer we must cry mightily, with fixedness of thought, firmness of faith, and devout affections. It concerns us in prayer to stir up all that is within us. It is not enough to fast for sin, but we must fast from sin; and, in order to the success of our prayers, we must no more regard iniquity in our hearts, [Ps.66.18] Psa 66:18. The work of a fast-day is not done with the day. The Ninevites hoped that God would turn from his fierce anger; and that thus their ruin would be prevented. They could not be so confident of finding mercy upon their repentance, as we may be, who have the death and merits of Christ, to which we may trust for pardon upon repentance. They dared not presume, but they did not despair. Hope of mercy is the great encouragement to repentance and reformation. Let us boldly cast ourselves down at the footstool of free grace, and God will look upon us with compassion. God sees who turn from their evil ways, and who do not. Thus he spared Nineveh. We read of no sacrifices offered to God to make atonement for sin; but a broken and a contrite heart, such as the Ninevites then had, he will not despise.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJonah repines at God's mercy to Nineveh, and is reproved.1–4He is taught by the withering of a gourd, that he did wrong.5–11
Jonah resents God's mercy (verses 1–4)

God's people usually celebrate and praise his mercy toward sinners.

But Jonah made that mercy the reason for accusing God.

He spoke as though showing compassion were a defect in God's nature, when it is actually one of his greatest glories.

We all owe our rescue from judgment to his pardoning, sparing mercy.

Jonah wished for death.

Henry calls that wish foolish, passionate and deeply corrupted.

Pride and lack of charity remained within the prophet.

He had neither expected nor desired Nineveh's salvation, but had only wanted to announce and witness its destruction.

He had not been humbled enough concerning his own sins.

Nor had he entrusted his personal honor and safety to the Lord.

In this frame of mind he failed to see the great good accomplished through his service and the glory of God's mercy.

We should frequently examine ourselves.

Is this the right thing to say or do?

Can I justify the way I am acting?

Is it right to become angry so quickly, so often or for so long?

Is it right to insult other people during anger?

Is it right to resent God's mercy toward repentant sinners?

That was Jonah's sin.

How could we resent something that glorifies God and advances his kingdom?

The conversion of sinners brings joy in heaven.

It should bring joy to us, not grief.

God teaches Jonah through the plant (verses 5–11)

Jonah went outside Nineveh but stayed near the city, apparently still wishing to see it destroyed.

People who habitually complain often create troubles for themselves so that they will always have something to resent.

Notice God's tenderness toward his people even when they are foolish and stubborn.

A small gift received at exactly the needed moment can become an enormous blessing.

A gourd in the right place may help us more than a cedar tree.

Even the smallest creatures can become great troubles or great comforts, depending on God's purpose.

People ruled by intense passions may be thrown down by a tiny disappointment or lifted up by a tiny pleasure.

Created comforts are perishable.

A small worm at the root can destroy a large and useful plant.

So our earthly comforts may disappear even when we cannot discover the immediate cause.

Sometimes the gift remains with us, but the joy it brought is gone.

The creature remains, but the comfort has disappeared.

God sent a wind that made Jonah feel the plant's absence.

Those who love to complain will find no shortage of things to complain about.

When Providence removes loved ones, possessions and pleasures, we must not resent God.

The strongest reason to silence our complaining is this:

When our gourd is gone, our God has not gone.

Jonah treated sin and death lightly while angry.

But one soul is worth more than the whole world, and certainly more than many plants and earthly comforts.

We should care more about our own and others' immortal souls than about the wealth and enjoyment of the world.

God's readiness to show mercy gives us every reason to hope.

Those who grumble may want God's grace reserved only for themselves and people like them.

But one Lord governs all people and is rich in mercy toward everyone who calls upon him.

When we are astonished at God's patience toward this stubborn prophet, let us examine our own hearts.

Remember our own ingratitude and obstinacy, and marvel at how patiently God deals with us.
classic_reading:
[Jonah.4.1-Jonah.4.4]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Jonah repines at God's mercy to Nineveh, and is reproved. | (1-4) |
He is taught by the withering of a gourd, that he did wrong. | (5-11) |
Verses 1-4
What all the saints make matter of joy and praise, Jonah makes the subject of reflection upon God; as if showing mercy were an imperfection of the Divine nature, which is the greatest glory of it. It is to his sparing, pardoning mercy, we all owe it that we are out of hell. He wishes for death: this was the language of folly, passion, and strong corruption. There appeared in Jonah remains of a proud, uncharitable spirit; and that he neither expected nor desired the welfare of the Ninevites, but had only come to declare and witness their destruction. He was not duly humbled for his own sins, and was not willing to trust the Lord with his credit and safety. In this frame of mind, he overlooked the good of which he had been an instrument, and the glory of the Divine mercy. We should often ask ourselves, Is it well to say thus, to do thus? Can I justify it? Do I well to be so soon angry, so often angry, so long angry, and to give others ill language in my anger? Do I well to be angry at the mercy of God to repenting sinners? That was Jonah's crime. Do we do well to be angry at that which is for the glory of God, and the advancement of his kingdom? Let the conversion of sinners, which is the joy of heaven, be our joy, and never our grief.
[Jonah.4.5-Jonah.4.11]
Verses 5-11
Jonah went out of the city, yet remained near at hand, as if he expected and desired its overthrow. Those who have fretful, uneasy spirits, often make troubles for themselves, that they may still have something to complain of. See how tender God is of his people in their afflictions, even though they are foolish and froward. A thing small in itself, yet coming seasonably, may be a valuable blessing. A gourd in the right place may do us more service than a cedar. The least creatures may be great plagues, or great comforts, as God is pleased to make them. Persons of strong passions are apt to be cast down with any trifle that crosses them, or to be lifted up with a trifle that pleases them. See what our creature-comforts are, and what we may expect them to be; they are withering things. A small worm at the root destroys a large gourd: our gourds wither, and we know not what is the cause. Perhaps creature-comforts are continued to us, but are made bitter; the creature is continued, but the comfort is gone. God prepared a wind to make Jonah feel the want of the gourd. It is just that those who love to complain, should never be left without something to complain of. When afflicting providences take away relations, possessions, and enjoyments, we must not be angry at God. What should especially silence discontent, is, that when our gourd is gone, our God is not gone. Sin and death are very dreadful, yet Jonah, in his heat, makes light of both. One soul is of more value than the whole world; surely then one soul is of more value than many gourds: we should have more concern for our own and others' precious souls, than for the riches and enjoyments of this world. It is a great encouragement to hope we shall find mercy with the Lord, that he is ready to show mercy. And murmurers shall be made to understand, that how willing soever they are to keep the Divine grace to themselves and those of their own way, there is one Lord over all, who is rich in mercy to all that call upon him. Do we wonder at the forbearance of God towards his perverse servant? Let us study our own hearts and ways; let us not forget our own ingratitude and obstinacy; and let us be astonished at God's patience towards us.
